summary: Defines MIB objects for managing the configuration, monitoring and control of Physical Units and Logical Units in an SNA environment, using SMIv2. It was a standards-track proposal. It was replaced by RFC 1666.

eli5.summary: Gauges for checking parts of an older IBM network. A newer version replaced it.

questions: what is an sna logical unit
how does snmp manage sna networks
what are response time monitor statistics
what information can be controlled in the snanau mib
subtitle: SNMP gauges for monitoring and controlling old IBM SNA networks.

tldr.problem: Network administrators lack standardized SNMP management objects to monitor and configure the Physical Units and Logical Units that form the core of SNA networks.
tldr.mechanism: Defines a set of managed objects (MIB tables) using SMIv2 that allow SNMP agents to report and modify the configuration, state, and statistics of SNA nodes, terminals, and sessions.
tldr.outcome: Enables centralized monitoring of SNA network resources, session state, performance statistics, and remote configuration changes. Replaced by RFC 1666.

today: RFC 1665 was a Proposed Standard published in July 1994 and was replaced by RFC 1666. While superseded, it remains historically important for understanding how SNA networks were managed via SNMP before the update.

sections.title: SNA Network Structure and Management Needs
sections.content:
Systems Network Architecture (SNA) is IBM's traditional network framework in which communication occurs between Network Addressable Units (NAUs). The two primary types of NAUs are Physical Units (PUs), which represent physical network nodes such as terminals and controller devices, and Logical Units (LUs), which represent the endpoints for application-to-application communication.

This RFC defines SNMP MIB objects for managing PU types 1.0, 2.0, and 2.1, as well as LU types 0 through 4, 7, and 6.2. Prior to this standard, network administrators had no uniform way to monitor SNA network configurations, session status, error conditions, or performance through standard SNMP management tools, making it difficult to manage large or distributed SNA networks effectively.
sections.eli5: Old IBM mainframe networks have computers (Physical Units) and programs (Logical Units) that talk to each other. Administrators needed a way to check on them and control them using standard network management tools.

sections.title: SNANAU MIB Structure and Table Organization
sections.content:
The SNANAU MIB module is organized into three major groups of managed objects. The snaNode group contains tables for managing SNA nodes, including the snaNodeAdminTable (configuration parameters), the snaNodeOperTable (current runtime values), the snaPu20StatsTable (statistics for PU 2.0 devices), and link association tables. The snaLu group manages Logical Units through the snaLuAdminTable (LU configuration), snaLuOperTable (operational state), snaLuSessnTable (session state), and snaLuSessnStatsTable (session statistics). The snaMgtTools group, which is optional, provides Response Time Monitor (RTM) statistics for LU type 2 devices.

Each object table is organized into "Admin" and "Oper" variants. Admin tables contain configuration parameters that can be modified by management stations and control the desired state of resources. Oper tables are extensions of the corresponding Admin tables and contain actual runtime values observed by the SNMP agent, which cannot be directly modified.
sections.eli5: The MIB is organized into three groups: one for controlling computers on the network, one for controlling programs on those computers, and an optional one for checking how fast messages are being answered.

sections.title: Configuration and Operational Control
sections.content:
Management stations can create, modify, and delete entries in the Admin tables to define new SNA nodes and logical units or adjust their configuration parameters. The snaNodeAdminIndex uniquely identifies each node, while objects like snaNodeAdminName specify the node's network name, and snaNodeAdminType specifies whether it is a PU 1.0, PU 2.0, PU 2.1, or other node type.

The AdminState object controls whether a node should be in the active or inactive operational state. When a node is activated via the Admin table, the SNMP agent automatically creates a corresponding entry in the Oper table with an initial OperState of "inactive". The agent then handles state transitions according to defined state diagrams. Similarly, RowStatus objects manage the creation and deletion of table entries.

For sessions, the MIB tracks state transitions from unbound through pending-bind, bound, and pending-unbind states. The agent automatically removes session entries when they return to the unbound state.
sections.eli5: Administrators can create new computers and programs, turn them on and off, and read back what the actual current state is, including what sessions are running.

sections.title: Monitoring and Statistics
sections.content:
The MIB provides extensive monitoring capabilities for observing network behavior. The snaPu20StatsTable contains counters and statistics specific to PU 2.0 devices, allowing administrators to track the operational history and performance of those nodes. Session statistics in the snaLuSessnStatsTable provide per-session information such as message counts, byte transfers, and error indicators.

The optional snaLuRtmTable offers Response Time Monitor (RTM) variables for LU type 2 devices, enabling administrators to measure how long it takes for transactions to complete. Session-level monitoring allows administrators to observe which sessions are active, their current state, and their operational parameters, providing visibility into the data flows within the SNA network.

The MIB also defines several traps (notifications) that the agent can send when significant events occur: Node state change events, Node activation failures, LU state changes, and LU session BIND failures alert administrators to important network events.
sections.eli5: Administrators can see counts of messages sent and received, check if any errors happened, measure how fast the network is responding, and get alerts when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Compliance and Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC defines conformance units that specify which groups of objects are mandatory or conditional. The snaNodeGroup, snaLuGroup, and snaSessionGroup are unconditionally mandatory for any implementation. The snaPu20Group is mandatory only for agents that manage PU type 2.0 devices, and the snaMgtToolsRtmGroup is mandatory only for those implementing LU type 2 with RTM support.

Agents may support either full row creation and deletion or at minimum support row modification. The specification notes that agents not implementing full row creation must at least support the ability to modify existing entries. This flexibility allows implementations to range from simple read-only agents for monitoring existing configurations to full-featured agents that support dynamic network reconfiguration.
sections.eli5: Different implementations can support different features—some just report information, others can create and delete entries. A basic implementation must support all the main features, with optional features only when the hardware supports them.
